w002: Advanced composites are foundational materials for aviation, space, shipbuilding and high-end industrial equipment. Despite rapid domestic growth, the industry has long faced missing supply-chain provenance, difficult quality-rights verification, information asymmetry, mismatched capacity, inefficient research commercialization, barriers to collaboration and insufficiently standardized repair services.
w003: Advanced Composites Protocol (ACP) builds on the established integrated composites R&D and application project comprising the Beijing R&D Center and Kaijiang Production Base. It brings civil-military integrated research, manufacturing, repair and technology commercialization capabilities on-chain. Blockchain provides trusted end-to-end provenance and quality verification for carbon fiber, resin, finished components and repair orders. RWA tokenization maps components, repair services, patents and research outcomes into on-chain assets. Smart contracts automate order fulfillment, service settlement and research revenue allocation. DAO governance brings together global research institutions, manufacturers, equipment users and technical talent for collaborative R&D, crowdfunded projects and shared proceeds.
w004: Initially, the protocol focuses on deploying physical capacity and mapping assets on-chain for civil aviation, commercial space, lightweight shipbuilding and industrial corrosion protection. In the medium to long term, it will build a decentralized manufacturing network and cross-chain data interoperability, becoming Web3 infrastructure for high-end equipment materials and promoting domestic production, scale and global collaboration in advanced composites.
w007: Aerospace, commercial space and lightweight shipbuilding continue to drive demand for high-performance resin-based and carbon-fiber composites. Large-scale production of large-tow carbon fiber significantly lowers raw-material costs, strengthening the economics of replacing traditional materials and opening an industrialization opportunity. Civil-military integration is rapidly increasing demand for lifecycle services from R&D and manufacturing to use, repair and maintenance, creating a clear market for integrated industry platforms.
w009: (1) Insufficient supply-chain trust: transfers of carbon fiber, resin and other key materials lack tamper-resistant records. Tracing component quality is difficult, and establishing and evidencing quality is costly in high-reliability applications such as aerospace.
w010: (2) Weak asset liquidity: high-end composite components, repair services and research patents are valuable physical assets with limited standardization. They are difficult to transfer, collateralize and share, and research commercialization takes a long time.
w011: (3) Capacity mismatch and information silos: fragmented information among research institutions, production bases and equipment users prevents idle capacity and research capabilities from efficiently meeting demand, wasting resources.
w012: (4) Missing research collaboration mechanisms: investment and proceeds in cross-institutional R&D depend on offline contracts with high fulfillment costs. Crowdfunded research is difficult to implement, and contributions cannot be quantified and verified.
w013: (5) Opaque repair and maintenance: in-house and field work orders, inspection reports and repair records are mostly offline documents that can be altered, making complete equipment lifecycle records difficult to retain.
w014: (6) Insufficient incentives: technical talent and partner institutions struggle to earn sustained, transparent returns on their contributions, weakening the drive for technical iteration.
w016: Bring physical business processes, assets and contributions on-chain: use blockchain immutability for provenance and rights verification, RWA tokenization for asset liquidity, smart contracts for automated fulfillment and revenue sharing, and DAOs for collaborative governance, connecting industry with on-chain networks.
w019: Build a decentralized full-lifecycle advanced composites protocol deeply integrating industry and Web3. Connect raw-material provenance, component R&D and manufacturing, repair and maintenance, and research commercialization in a complete loop. Address information asymmetry, capacity mismatch and slow commercialization while supporting domestic production, scale and global collaboration.
w021: The world’s first decentralized R&D and application protocol focused on the full lifecycle of advanced composites, serving as Web3 infrastructure for high-end equipment materials. Its physical foundation is the integrated composites R&D and application project (Beijing R&D Center + Kaijiang Production Base); its on-chain layer consists of the ACP blockchain protocol, smart contracts, RWA assets and DAO governance.
w023: (1) Short term (0–12 months): bring base operations on-chain, trace materials, components and repair orders, and implement the first RWA mappings.
w024: (2) Medium term (12–24 months): establish a global collaborative DAO research network, enable research crowdfunding and asset transfers, and form a decentralized manufacturing collaboration network.
w025: (3) Long term (after 24 months): achieve cross-chain interoperability, establish industry standards and become on-chain collaboration infrastructure for the global composites industry.
w027: (1) Physical assets first: all on-chain assets are anchored to real-world capacity, products and services, rejecting purely virtual speculation detached from industry.
w028: (2) Compliance first: distinguish governance credentials from physical transactions. Civil-military operations strictly follow domestic R&D and production qualifications, confidentiality, airworthiness and national military standards requirements.
w029: (3) Open source and participation: open-source core smart contracts and encourage ecosystem involvement. Classified civil-military source data remains off-chain; only hash evidence is stored on-chain.
w030: Industrial foundation: the Beijing–Sichuan integrated composites R&D and application platform
w031: ACP is not a purely on-chain project: every on-chain activity is anchored to offline project capabilities. Its physical foundation operates through an integrated model of research in Beijing, production in Kaijiang and service across regions, with the following capabilities.
w033: The Beijing R&D Center handles technology research, new-product prototyping, advanced talent and patent development. The Kaijiang Production Base handles component manufacturing, in-house repair, volume production, warehousing and logistics, creating complementary capabilities between Beijing and Sichuan.
w035: (1) Custom composite manufacturing: standardized custom manufacture of composite articles, parts, components and supporting spares for equipment across multiple sectors.
w036: (2) Precision in-house and emergency field repairs: repair composite components in the workshop or at the operating site to maintain equipment reliability.
w037: (3) New composite manufacturing processes: develop innovative fabrication technologies for new composite components and address industry technical challenges.
w038: (4) Efficient aviation composite repair R&D: specifically research and optimize efficient aviation composite repair technologies to improve the high-end repair technology system.
w040: (1) Civil and general aviation: growing domestic fleets and general-aviation aircraft inventories drive increasing annual demand for fuselage, wing and interior component manufacturing and periodic repairs.
w041: (2) Commercial space: increasing demand for carbon-fiber structural components for satellites and launch vehicles creates a broad market for high-performance volume manufacturing.
w042: (3) Lightweight shipbuilding: lightweighting and corrosion-protection upgrades are replacing traditional metal marine components with composites at an increasing rate.
w043: (4) Industrial corrosion protection: oil pipelines, corrosion-resistant industrial equipment and lightweight equipment steadily increase demand for composite products.
w045: The core team has years of aerospace composite R&D, manufacturing and quality-management experience. It understands national military-standard quality systems and civil-aircraft airworthiness management. Core staff have participated throughout quality control for several key national equipment programs and possess mature aviation-grade quality capabilities. Experience in standardized state-owned enterprise management and efficient private-sector operations supports a standardized, precise and efficient quality model that safeguards product stability and reliability.
w047: Initial project investment is approximately RMB 50 million, mainly for production equipment, factory rental and standardized refurbishment. The initial Kaijiang plant plan covers 200 m²: 160 m² for equipment operation, a 10 m² cleanroom, 10 m² of raw-material cold storage and 20 m² of support space. Core equipment includes ovens, winding machines, curing furnaces, field repair kits and a complete set of tooling. Beijing uses a fixed-core-team plus flexible-talent model, with 3 full-time technical leads and initially 5 permanent specialist operators, adding advanced talent as needed. The project will steadily pursue R&D and production qualifications to strengthen compliant operations.
w048: Important: classified original defense-related business data is never stored on-chain in plaintext. Only hashes, work-order numbers and asset IDs are recorded on-chain; classified source data stays in secure offline systems.
w049: ACP protocol design and technical architecture
w050: The architecture comprises four layers: physical sensing, an off-chain evidence gateway, the core blockchain protocol and application interfaces.
w053: Covers all production and inspection equipment, warehousing, repair-order systems, patent archives and materials inventory systems at Beijing and Kaijiang. It captures carbon-fiber/resin batches, component process records, curing inspection data, in-house/field repairs, patent documents and capacity ledgers. Original data remains offline; data fingerprints (hashes) pass through the gateway for on-chain evidence. Classified plaintext is never uploaded.
w055: Middleware between industry and blockchain computes business-data hashes and verifies signatures, verifies physical RWA assets and rights, synchronizes physical orders and repair status on-chain, redacts and isolates sensitive classified data, and connects IoT devices for automatic reporting of material receipt, component dispatch and repair completion.
w056: Key security mechanism: the gateway supports multisignature review. RWA minting requires joint signatures from at least 2 authorized physical-project managers to prevent fictitious assets from entering the chain.
w058: Blockchain selection uses a consortium-chain + public-chain hybrid. The consortium chain records domestic civil-military business evidence to meet regulatory, graded cybersecurity protection and confidentiality requirements. Public chains support RWA tokens, DAO governance and global collaboration, with bridges enabling cross-chain interoperability.
w060: (1) Raw-material provenance: records batches, suppliers, receipt and consumption; each carbon-fiber or resin batch receives a unique on-chain ID with hash evidence throughout transfers, allowing component materials to be traced.
w061: (2) Component lifecycle: records states from prototyping, production and dispatch to operation, factory repair and retirement, linking inspection-report hashes to establish quality evidence.
w062: (3) RWA issuance: standardizes minting, redemption and burning, anchored to components, repair packages and patent assets.
w063: (4) Orders and repairs: automatically records field/in-house repair orders and executes settlement when stage conditions are met.
w064: (5) Research crowdfunding and revenue allocation: the DAO initiates collaborative research, records contributions and distributes project proceeds automatically under preset rules.
w065: (6) DAO governance: proposal submission, voting, weight calculation, execution and governance-parameter management.
w066: (7) Cross-chain interoperability (phase two): enables ACP assets and evidence data to interact across chains with other Web3 infrastructure.
w068: Role-specific portals include the industrial administration console (gateway management, RWA verification), equipment-user portal (provenance queries, manufacturing/repair orders), DAO governance portal (proposals, crowdfunding, voting) and RWA marketplace (display and transfer of rights credentials; physical delivery still follows offline commercial procedures).
w071: (1) Trusted lifecycle provenance: immutable on-chain hashes across materials, manufacturing, use, repairs and retirement support airworthiness and military-standard quality evidence.
w072: (2) Two-way RWA anchoring: each on-chain RWA credential maps to one offline asset; burning corresponds to completed delivery or retirement of that asset.
w073: (3) Contribution quantification: research output, process improvements and supplied capacity are marked on-chain as inputs to DAO voting weight and revenue allocation.
w074: (4) Classified-data isolation: defense-related classified activities store only hashes on-chain, with plaintext offline, strictly respecting confidentiality rules.
w076: ACP RWA are not the physical objects themselves, but credentials for rights, services and proceeds. Physical delivery, logistics, acceptance and compliant transactions take place offline; rights and status are recorded on-chain.

w095: Figure 1. ACP business loop: material provenance → component R&D and manufacturing → repair and maintenance → research commercialization
w096: (1) Offline verification: physical project operators verify the authenticity of materials, components, patents and capacity.
w097: (2) Gateway multisignature review: at least 2 authorized managers jointly sign confirmation.
w098: (3) Smart contracts mint the corresponding RWA credential, bind a unique physical ID and record it in the provenance contract.
w099: (4) Rights credentials may circulate on-chain; physical transactions, logistics and acceptance occur offline.
w100: (5) Consumption/retirement: RWA credentials are burned on-chain when components retire, services finish or patents expire.
w101: Restriction: classified civil-military physical assets do not receive transferable RWA. Only on-chain hash evidence is allowed; tokenized circulation is not opened.
w103: Important: the ACP protocol token is for ecosystem governance and business utility, is not a security and promises no returns. It does not represent equity in the physical company; industrial operating proceeds are isolated from the token. Symbol: ACP.
w105: (1) DAO voting: holding/staking ACP provides voting weight for protocol parameters, ecosystem grants and research-crowdfunding proposals.
w106: (2) Ecosystem participation: collaborative research crowdfunding requires staking ACP.
w107: (3) Incentives: rewards research contributors, capacity providers and ecosystem builders.
w108: (4) Protocol fees: RWA minting and proposal creation consume small amounts of ACP, part of which is burned for deflation.
w109: (5) Staking returns: staking, locking and providing liquidity earn protocol incentives, giving ACP both governance and revenue-related utility.

w138: (1) RWA minting and proposal creation charge small ACP fees: 50% is burned directly and 50% enters the DAO treasury.
w139: (2) A portion of on-chain research-project proceeds returns to the treasury for ongoing R&D incentives.
w140: (3) Tokens are not used to purchase physical military equipment or classified supplies. Physical products continue to settle offline in fiat currency.
w142: ACP is both an on-chain governance credential and an asset capable of earning incentives within the protocol. Holders may stake through different DeFi mechanisms to obtain on-chain rewards, creating a token-use loop driven by governance and proceeds.
w143: (1) Staking governance (veACP model): users lock ACP to obtain veACP governance credentials, with voting-weight amplification of up to 1–3 times. Protocol fee shares depend on staked amounts and lock durations and come from a portion of RWA minting, proposal and asset-transfer fees.
w144: (2) RWA revenue-pool staking: staking ACP in RWA pools provides proportional participation in on-chain RWA-related service proceeds, including repair-service fulfillment fees and the on-chain distributable portion of patent licensing revenue, combining asset-derived proceeds and on-chain incentives.
w145: (3) Liquidity mining: provide liquidity for ACP/stablecoin pairs to receive liquidity rewards and trading-fee shares, supporting liquidity and market depth.
w146: (4) Locking: flexible staking and fixed-term locking are supported. Longer locks have higher reward coefficients, encouraging long-term holding and smoothing market fluctuations.
w147: Sources and separation: all staking rewards come from on-chain protocol fees, DAO treasury ecosystem budgets and liquidity incentives, strictly separated from corporate operating profits. No fixed rate of return is promised; rewards vary with on-chain activity and governance decisions.
w149: Offline operating profits belong to the physical composites enterprise and are not directly distributed to token holders. Holders receive only protocol governance rights and ecosystem incentives. Smart contracts allocate crowdfunded research proceeds to participants under legally executed offline agreements; tokens serve only as on-chain accounting credentials.
w151: ACP-DAO governs the protocol through a hybrid model. Physical project operators hold veto rights over civil-military confidentiality matters and major physical capacity investments; ordinary ecosystem, research and parameter proposals are decided by community vote.
w153: (1) Core industrial council: the Beijing and Kaijiang project entities verify asset authenticity and manage classified risks, with veto rights on high-risk proposals.
w154: (2) Research institutions: universities and composites institutes contribute processes and patented technologies and may initiate crowdfunded R&D proposals.
w155: (3) Industrial partners: equipment makers and space, aviation and shipbuilding users contribute market demand, orders and applications.
w156: (4) Community contributors: engineers, developers and ecosystem participants stake ACP for voting rights.

w159: (2) Ecosystem grants: support developers and partners expanding ACP.
w160: (3) Protocol parameters: modify fees, staking weights and RWA contract parameters.
w161: (4) RWA admission: add a new asset standard.

w164: (1) Voting weight = staked-ACP weight + weighted research contribution, encouraging real technical input rather than token ownership alone.
w165: (2) Ordinary proposals pass with the required quorum and majority approval.
w166: (3) High-risk proposals (new major RWA categories or large treasury spending) require greater participation and no industrial-council veto.

w169: The treasury holds ACP. All spending must be executed through on-chain proposal voting, with publicly traceable flows. Treasury funds serve only the protocol ecosystem, not routine production or operating costs at physical bases.
w172: Carbon fiber and resin receive on-chain IDs on arrival. Each component’s process-data hashes are recorded. After delivery to aviation/satellite companies, users can retrieve complete provenance histories to support airworthiness and military-standard quality audits. Repair records are appended to the same ID when components return, retaining the entire lifecycle history.
w173: Scenario two: composite repair-service RWA matching
w174: Aviation and shipbuilding companies buy standardized repair-service RWA credentials. Equipment faults trigger work orders and smart contracts dispatch in-house repairs at Kaijiang or field teams. Completion automatically consumes the service credentials;
w175: all repair records go on-chain, addressing slow response and opaque service processes.
w177: Research institutions submit DAO proposals for new composites and request treasury funding. Multiple institutions and engineers participate, with smart contracts recording contributions. Resulting patents become technology RWA, and commercialization proceeds are automatically allocated to all contributors under prior agreements, addressing difficult investment allocation and slow commercialization.
w179: Beijing prototyping and Kaijiang production capacity generate RWA quotas. Enterprises needing temporary prototypes or small batches can buy capacity RWA to call idle resources, helping absorb surplus capacity and reduce mismatches.
w181: ACP connects compliant composites production bases across China and globally, each mapping its capacity into RWA;
w182: equipment users publish requirements and the DAO coordinates the best production match, forming a distributed decentralized manufacturing network.

w199: (1) Strictly follow regulations on civil-military integration, R&D/production licensing, confidentiality, airworthiness and national military-standard quality management.
w200: (2) Do not market the token as a financial investment product; clarify its governance and utility role only.
w201: (3) RWA are rights credentials only; physical asset trading, logistics, taxation and contracts remain offline.
w202: (4) Conduct regular contract security audits and publish reports.
w203: (5) Staking incentives apply only to protocol participation, with no fixed-return promise or disguised financing. Mechanisms undergo legal and compliance review before launch.

w215: (2) Industrial clients: civil aviation, commercial space, shipbuilding and industrial equipment firms use RWA services.
w216: (3) Manufacturing: composites production bases join the decentralized manufacturing network in future.

w220: ACP combines the Beijing–Kaijiang physical civil-military composites capabilities with blockchain, RWA and DAO governance. It drives on-chain innovation from industrial demand rather than concepts detached from industry.
w221: The protocol addresses difficult provenance, mismatched capacity and slow commercialization, connecting the full lifecycle of advanced composites from raw materials to repairs and retirement. With strict compliance and confidentiality, it enables industry and Web3 to reinforce each other, supports domestic production and scale, and explores a new model of global collaboration for high-end equipment materials.

f001: Full diagram description: four layers run from top to bottom. Application interfaces: industrial administration, equipment-user portal, DAO portal and RWA market. Core protocol: raw-material provenance, component lifecycle, RWA issuance, orders/repairs, research crowdfunding, DAO governance and cross-chain interoperability (phase two). ACP-Gateway: data hashes and signature checks, physical RWA rights verification, work-order synchronization, classified-data redaction/isolation and automatic IoT reports. Physical sensing: Beijing/Kaijiang production equipment, inspection, warehousing, repair orders, patent archives and inventory movements. Security baseline: multiple contract audits, bug bounties, multisignature controls and no classified plaintext on-chain. Boundary: on-chain rights credentials and hash evidence only, without intervening in physical operations.
f002: Full diagram description: the physical layer contains material provenance (carbon-fiber/resin batch hashes), component R&D/manufacturing (process data on-chain), repair/maintenance (in-house and field work-order evidence) and commercialization (patents and agreed revenue allocation). Physical data passes through ACP-Gateway with hashes and multisignature verification into the evidence/RWA layer: component rights and lifecycle histories, repair-capacity credentials, partial patent revenue rights, and manufacturing/prototyping quotas. RWA rights credentials participate in staking, proceeds and governance. The protocol/DAO layer runs through veACP locking (amount × term × participation time), weighted calculation (Boost multiplier), revenue distribution (treasury rewards) and DAO voting (proposals, parameters, grants). The protocol treasury contains fees, staking incentives and the DAO ecosystem budget, strictly separated from physical operating profits.
